title: Pushing to GitHub
objectives: Connect a remote and push your work
Say what push, fetch and pull each move
Recover when your laptop and origin have drifted apart

screens.title: Pushing to GitHub
screens.prose: Your commits live on one laptop, and laptops get lost. We will keep a second copy on GitHub and keep the two in step.
Your returns project lives on your laptop as four commits, A to D. Last week you also put a copy on GitHub. It stopped at commit B.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: Top row: your laptop. Bottom row: the copy on GitHub.

screens.question: Your laptop is stolen tonight. Tap the commits you lose for good.

hints.text: Which commits exist in only one place?
GitHub has these two.
A and B survive on GitHub. C and D exist only on the laptop.

feedback.correct: C and D exist only on the laptop, so they go with it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A commit is lost only if no other copy of it exists.

byKey.all-local: You picked every commit on the laptop. A and B also sit on GitHub, so they survive.
byKey.newest: You picked only the newest. C is missing from GitHub too.
byKey.LA: A is on GitHub as well, so a copy survives.
byKey.LB: B is on GitHub as well, so a copy survives.
byKey.OA: That is GitHub's copy of A. It is not on the laptop, so a theft cannot touch it.
byKey.OB: That is GitHub's copy of B. It is not on the laptop, so a theft cannot touch it.

explain.text: You picked the commits with no second copy. GitHub holds A and B, so only C and D are at risk. Keeping GitHub up to date shrinks that risk to nothing.

screens.prose:
You run one command to bring GitHub up to date:

```sh
$ git push
```

Watch the bottom row.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: Top row: your laptop. Bottom row: the copy on GitHub.

screens.question: Tap the commits that `git push` copied to GitHub.

hints.text: Which commits are new in the bottom row?
These arrived after the push.

feedback.correct: Push copied C and D, the commits GitHub lacked.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the commits that appeared in the bottom row.

byKey.top: Those are the laptop's own commits. Push leaves them where they are and sends copies.
byKey.OA: A was on GitHub already, so push had nothing to send.
byKey.OB: B was on GitHub already, so push had nothing to send.

explain.text: Push sent only what GitHub lacked: C and D. The laptop keeps its commits. Now both rows match, so a stolen laptop costs you nothing.

screens.prose:
GitHub's copy is a **remote**, a repository somewhere else that you send commits to. By convention it is called `origin`. Now you set up a new laptop:

```sh
$ git clone https://github.com/ana/returns-project.git
```

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: Top row: the new laptop, still empty. Bottom row: origin.

screens.question: What does the new laptop have after the clone?

options.text: Commits A to D, the files as of D, and `origin` set up
Only the files as of D, with no history
options.why: You expected a download of files. A clone copies every commit, so the whole history comes too.

options.text: Commit D alone
options.why: You copied only the newest commit. D points back to C, and the clone brings that whole chain.

options.text: An empty folder linked to GitHub
options.why: You expected the copy to wait for a pull. Clone downloads everything at once.

hints.text: Clone means copy. A copy of what?
This is everything the remote holds.
Clone copies the whole chain, A to D, and remembers where it came from as `origin`.

feedback.correct: A clone is a full copy: every commit, plus a link back called origin.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A clone copies the whole repository.

explain.text: `git clone` copied all four commits and checked out D's files. It also set `origin` to the address you cloned from. So `git push` from the new laptop already knows where to go.

canvas.caption: The clone: the same four commits

screens.prose: Both rows match. You fix the volatility scaling in `returns.py`, from 250 to 252 trading days. You save the file, skip the commit and run `git push`.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: Top row: your laptop. Bottom row: the copy on GitHub.

screens.question: What does GitHub hold after this push?

options.text: Commits A to D only: the fix stays on your laptop
Commit D with your saved fix added to it
options.why: You expected push to send your saved files. Push sends commits, and a commit never changes once made.

options.text: A new commit E holding the fix
options.why: You expected push to commit for you. Only `git commit` makes a commit, and you skipped it.

options.text: Nothing, because push refuses while files are unsaved
options.why: The file is saved, and push does not check your folder at all. It compares commits only.

hints.text: What does push send: files or commits?
Your laptop has no commit after D.
The fix lives in a saved file, not in a commit. Push compares commits and finds nothing new.

feedback.correct: Push sends commits. An edit that is not committed goes nowhere.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which commits the laptop has that GitHub lacks.

byKey.file: You expected push to update D. A commit is fixed once made, and push sends only whole commits.
byKey.new: You expected push to make a commit. It never does; `git commit` does.

explain.text: Git prints `Everything up-to-date`, because both rows end at D. Your fix is a saved change, not a commit. Commit it first, then push.

screens.prose:
Overnight your colleague Sam pushed commit E: trading costs of 5 bp per trade. You download it with

```sh
$ git fetch
```

Fetch brings new commits from origin onto your laptop.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: Top row: your laptop. Bottom row: the copy on GitHub.

screens.question: After the fetch, does `returns.py` in your folder charge trading costs?

options.text: No: E is downloaded, but your files still match D
Yes: fetch brings E's changes into your files
options.why: You treated fetch as an update of your folder. It only downloads; your branch and files stay at D.

options.text: Only if E clashes with your work
options.why: You expected fetch to merge. It never touches your files, clash or not.

hints.text: Fetch downloads. Does downloading change your files?
Your branch still ends here.
E now sits on your laptop as origin's latest commit, but your own branch still ends at D.

feedback.correct: Fetch downloads E and leaves your files alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fetch downloads commits and changes nothing else.

byKey.yes: You expected fetch to change your files. That second step is a merge, which fetch does not do.

explain.text: Fetch copied E to your laptop, but your branch still ends at D. You can read E first with `git log origin/main`. `git pull` does the fetch and then merges E into your branch.

canvas.caption: Fetched: E is on the laptop, but your branch still ends at D

screens.prose: Most days look the same. Get Sam's overnight commits, make your change, record it, share it.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: Start of the day: you have pulled nothing yet

screens.question: Put a day's work in order.

hints.text: What must happen before you can commit?
Pull first so you start from Sam's work. Then edit, stage, commit, and push last.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You can only push a commit, and only commit what you staged.

byKey.push: Push only sends commits that exist. It belongs after the commit.
byKey.pull: Pull belongs first, so your edit starts from Sam's latest commit.
byKey.add: Staging comes after the edit and before the commit.
byKey.commit: The commit records what you staged, so it follows `git add`.
byKey.edit: You can only stage a change once you have made it.

explain.text: Pulling first means your commit builds on Sam's latest work. Each later step needs the one before: stage the edit, commit it, push the commit. Push last, once the commit exists.

canvas.caption: F on both rows after the push

screens.prose: Another day. You commit F, a new signal, without pulling first. An hour earlier Sam pushed E, a cost fix. Both commits point back to D.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: The rows have drifted apart after D

screens.question: You run `git push`. What happens?

options.text: Git refuses, and origin is unchanged
F replaces E on origin
options.why: You expected push to overwrite. Git will not drop Sam's commit E without being forced.

options.text: F is added after E on origin
options.why: You expected F to queue up after E. F points back to D, so it cannot simply follow E.

options.text: Origin keeps both, side by side
options.why: You expected origin to hold two tips. A branch on origin ends at one commit, so Git refuses instead.

hints.text: If F went onto origin, what would happen to E?
F's arrow points here, not to E.
Origin's branch must end at one commit. Accepting F would throw away E, so Git refuses.

feedback.correct: Git rejects the push to keep Sam's commit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what origin would lose if it took F.

byKey.overwrite: You expected push to overwrite. Git refuses rather than discard someone's commit.

explain.text: Git prints `! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)`. Origin has a commit, E, that you do not. Bring E into your branch first, then push again.

screens.prose:
So you pull. You once ran `git config --global pull.rebase false`, which tells pull to merge when the rows have drifted apart. Without a setting, recent Git asks you to choose.

```sh
$ git pull
```

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: Your F and Sam's E both follow D

screens.question: What does your laptop's history look like after the pull?

options.text: A new commit M that joins F and E, so both are kept
Origin's chain, A to E: your F is gone
options.why: You expected pull to copy GitHub over your work. Pull never deletes your commits; F stays.

options.text: A, B, C, D, F, then E on the end
options.why: You expected E to slot in after F. E points back to D, so Git joins the two lines with a merge commit.

options.text: No change until you push
options.why: You expected pull to wait for a push. Pull changes your laptop straight away.

hints.text: Pull fetches E. Where can E go if F must stay?
Both of these point back to D.
Pull fetches E, then merges: Git makes a commit M with two parents, F and E.

feedback.correct: Pull fetched E, then merged it with F in a new commit M.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pull keeps your commits and adds Sam's.

byKey.replace: You expected pull to make your laptop a copy of GitHub. Pull adds commits; it never throws yours away.
byKey.line: You expected a straight line. E was made from D, not from F, so the lines must be joined by a merge.

explain.text: Pull fetched E, then merged it: M has two parents, your F and Sam's E. If both touched the same lines, you would resolve a conflict first. Then `git push` works, because origin's E is now in your history.

canvas.caption: After the pull: M joins F and E

screens.prose:
You have used all four commands that move commits between your laptop and a remote:

```sh
$ git clone <url>  # copy it, history and all
$ git push         # send new commits to origin
$ git fetch        # download; files untouched
$ git pull         # fetch, then merge
```

Push and pull move **commits**, never uncommitted edits.
screens.question: Which command can change the files in your project folder?

options.text: `git pull`
`git fetch`
options.why: You saw fetch download E while your files stayed at D. It never changes them.

options.text: `git push`
options.why: Push sends commits away. Your own files stay as they are.

hints.text: Which command includes a merge?
Pull is fetch plus merge, and the merge updates your files.

feedback.correct: Only pull merges, so only pull changes your files.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the command that merges.

explain.text: Fetch downloads and push uploads; neither touches your folder. Pull adds a merge, and the merge updates your files. That is why fetch is safe to run at any time.

screens.prose: Your push of a new momentum signal was rejected. Sam has pushed a cost change, and you want to see it before merging. You also test before sharing.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

screens.question: Put the commands in order.

lines.text: `git log -p origin/main`: read what it changed
`git merge origin/main`: join it to your work

hints.text: Which step needs Sam's commit on your laptop?
Download first, then read. Merge only after reading. Test the merged code, then push.

feedback.correct: Fetch, read, merge, test, push: a pull split in two, with a look in between.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the result of the one before.

byKey.log: You cannot read Sam's commit before fetch downloads it.
byKey.merge: Merge after reading, so you know what you are taking in.
byKey.test: Test the merged code, so it comes after the merge.
byKey.push: Push last, once the merged code passes its tests.
byKey.fetch: Fetch comes first: every other step needs Sam's commit on your laptop.

explain.text: Fetch and merge together are what pull does; splitting them lets you read Sam's change first. The tests run on the merged code, which nobody has run before. Then push sends F and the merge commit.

canvas.caption: After the merge: ready to test and push

screens.prose:
Your Stage 1 project computes returns, annualised volatility and maximum drawdown from SPY closes. It has six commits. You made an empty GitHub repository, `returns-project`, and ran `git push`:

```sh
$ git push
fatal: No configured push destination.
```

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: Six commits on the laptop; the GitHub repository is empty

screens.question: What fixes it?

options.text: `git remote add origin https://github.com/ana/returns-project.git`, then `git push -u origin main`
`git clone https://github.com/ana/returns-project.git`, then `git push`
options.why: You cloned the empty repository into a new folder. Your six commits stay in the old one.

options.text: `git commit -am "Publish"`, then `git push`
options.why: The commits already exist. What is missing is where to send them.

options.text: `git pull`
options.why: Pull also needs a remote, and this repository has none yet.

hints.text: Read the error: what has the push not got?
Git has no remote to push to. Add one called origin, then push main to it.

feedback.correct: Name the remote once, then push. `-u` makes later pushes need no names.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The error says Git has nowhere to push to.

byKey.clone: You cloned the empty repository. That makes a second, empty project and leaves your commits behind.

explain.text: `git remote add` gives the GitHub address the name origin. `git push -u origin main` sends all six commits and remembers the pairing. From then on, a plain `git push` works.

ideas: A remote is another copy of the repository. `git push` sends it the commits it lacks.
`git fetch` downloads commits and leaves your files alone. `git pull` fetches, then merges.
When both sides have new commits, push is refused. Pull to merge, test, then push.

formula.name: Pull
formula.note: Only the merge step changes your files.

summary.trap: Push sends commits, not saved files. An edit you never committed stays on your laptop.

quiz.prose: The repository on GitHub has 47 commits. You run `git clone` on a new machine.
quiz.question: How many commits does `git log` show on the new machine?

feedback.correct: All 47. A clone is a full copy.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a clone copies.

byKey.newest: You expected only the latest commit. A clone brings the whole history.

explain.text: A clone copies every commit, not only the newest files. So the history on the new machine is identical. That is why a clone is also a backup.

quiz.prose: You commit twice and push. Then you edit `signal.py`, save it and push again. A colleague clones the repository.
quiz.question: Does their `signal.py` have your latest edit?

options.text: No: the edit was never committed
Yes: the second push sent it
options.why: You expected push to send saved files. It sends commits, and the edit is in none.

options.text: Yes, but only after they pull
options.why: Pulling cannot fetch what was never pushed. The edit is only on your laptop.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which commits reached GitHub.

explain.text: The second push found no new commits and sent nothing. The edit exists only in your folder. Commit it, then push.

quiz.prose: You are in the middle of an edit and do not want your files to change. You want to see what Sam pushed this morning.
quiz.question: Which command downloads Sam's commits without touching your files?

options.text: `git fetch`
`git pull`
options.why: Pull also merges, and the merge changes your files.

options.text: `git clone`
options.why: Clone makes a whole new copy in a new folder. You already have the repository.

options.text: `git push`
options.why: Push sends your commits up. It downloads nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need a download with no merge.

explain.text: `git fetch` brings Sam's commits to your laptop and stops. Read them with `git log origin/main`. Merge later, when your edit is committed.

quiz.prose: Your laptop has two commits that origin lacks. Origin has three commits that your laptop lacks.
quiz.question: You run `git push`. What happens?

options.text: Rejected: pull first, then push
Your two commits are added on top of origin's three
options.why: Your commits point back to the old tip, not to origin's new ones. Git refuses rather than guess.

options.text: Origin's three commits are replaced by your two
options.why: Git will not throw away commits on origin unless you force it.

feedback.correct: Origin has work you lack, so the push is refused.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Origin would lose three commits if it took yours.

explain.text: Both sides moved on from the same commit. Origin refuses a push that would drop its three new commits. Pull to merge them in, then push.
